mcqs.question: Audio and video catalogs can land in a similar total-byte ballpark. What actually differs in how each system's scale challenge shows up?
options: Audio's challenge shows up as lookups per second from item count; video's shows up as bytes per second from item size
There is no meaningful difference between the two catalogs at any scale
Video has more total items than audio in every real deployment
Audio files require more storage per item than video renditions
mcqs.explanation: Audio reaches large catalog size through sheer item count (hundreds of millions of small tracks), so its pressure point is metadata QPS. Video reaches similar totals through per-item size (few, huge files), so its pressure point is egress bandwidth. Audio has far more items than video, and a single track is nowhere near a video rendition's size.

mcqs.question: Why must an offline-downloaded track's license expiry be enforced on the client device rather than solely by the server?
options: Servers are not capable of tracking subscription expiry dates
Client-side enforcement is required because playback must be blocked correctly even when the device has no connectivity to ask the server
License expiry only matters for streamed tracks, not downloaded ones
Clients are legally required to store all licensing logic
mcqs.explanation: The whole point of offline playback is that it works without connectivity, so the device itself must be able to determine and enforce that a license has lapsed — a server check alone can't run offline. Servers do track expiry (for refreshing valid licenses); this concern applies specifically to downloaded tracks; and it's a design necessity, not a legal mandate.

mcqs.question: Why does the metadata/catalog service typically need heavier caching and read scaling in an audio system than in a comparable video system?
options: Audio files are individually larger and take longer to look up
Video systems don't use a metadata service at all
Listeners generate many catalog lookups per minute (search, skip, queue) across a much larger item count, unlike one manifest lookup per long video session
Metadata lookups are more expensive computationally for audio than for video
mcqs.explanation: Audio listening behavior — constant skipping and searching across hundreds of millions of tracks — drives catalog QPS far above a video viewer's one-lookup-per-long-session pattern. Audio files are actually smaller, not larger; video systems do use a metadata service, just at lower QPS; and the per-lookup cost isn't inherently higher for audio, the volume is.

mcqs.question: Why is importing video's full adaptive-bitrate rendition ladder into an audio streaming design usually unnecessary?
options: A compressed audio track is small enough to fit in a phone's cache or RAM, so the network-adaptation machinery ABR exists for is largely unneeded
Audio playback never experiences network issues on any device
Adaptive bitrate techniques cannot technically be applied to audio codecs
Audio files never need more than one available bitrate under any circumstances
mcqs.explanation: ABR exists to survive a fluctuating network across a large chunked file; an audio track is small enough that a player can just fetch a couple of fixed bitrates and buffer the whole thing, making the full ABR machinery overkill. Network issues do exist for audio too, ABR is technically possible for audio, and some players do offer more than one bitrate — the point is the complexity isn't warranted at this file size.
